lead: Today, in the second week of the season of Annunciation, the Church honours the grace God gave to Mary at the first instant of her existence: she was preserved from every stain of original sin, by the merits of the Son she would one day bear. No reading states this doctrine in so many words. Together they prepare the ground for it. In Sirach, Wisdom looks for a resting place and God chooses her tent. In Isaiah, the Lord himself promises a sign: a woman and a son called Immanuel. In Hebrews, the Son who is the reflection of God's glory takes hold of our human race. In Luke, Mary herself sings and gives all the credit to “God my Savior”. The line runs from a tent, to a mother, to the Son, to her song, and its key words are dwelling, sign and mercy.

r.h: Wisdom looks for a resting place
set: Ben Sira, the son of Sirach, taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC. His grandson translated the book into Greek in Egypt some decades later, and tells us so in his prologue. Parts of the Hebrew have been recovered, but this chapter is known to us mainly through the Greek. Chapter 24 stands near the centre of the book. Wisdom, spoken of as a woman, praises herself before the heavenly court.

The speech has a clear aim. Greek culture was attractive to Jews of that time, and Ben Sira answers that the highest wisdom is not far away. A few verses after our reading he identifies her with the Law given through Moses (24:23). The one who ruled the whole world was given her home in Israel.
str: vv. 1–2: introduction: Wisdom speaks among her people and before the hosts of the Most High.
vv. 3–7: her origin and her search: from God's mouth, over all the earth, looking for a place to rest.
vv. 8–12: God's command: she pitches her tent in Jacob and is established in Zion.
vv. 13–14: she grows like the great trees of the land, from Lebanon and Hermon to En-gedi and Jericho.
kw: Here wisdom is more than cleverness. She is the plan and the skill by which God made and guides the world, spoken of as a person. The New Testament will call Christ “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).
The word for Israel's tent of meeting in the Greek Old Testament. John uses the related verb when he says the Word “lived among us”, literally pitched his tent (John 1:14).
She who rules every nation is still looking for somewhere to settle (v. 7). God's plan is told as a search for a home.
vv: Among all these I sought a resting place; in whose territory should I abide?
The great lady of the universe asks a homeless person's question. It prepares the surprise of the next verse.
Then the Creator of all things gave me a command, and my Creator chose the place for my tent.
Wisdom does not choose her own home; God chooses it for her. On this feast the Church hears a likeness: before the Word came, God prepared the place where he would dwell.
I took root in an honored people, in the portion of the Lord, his heritage.
The image moves from a tent to a tree. What came down from above now grows in the soil of one people. The Son of God too will have his roots in Israel, through a daughter of Israel.
ch: The first and literal sense of the chapter concerns Wisdom and the Law. Christians came to see its fullness in Christ, the Word who pitched his tent among us. The Church also applies such passages to Mary, not because Mary is divine Wisdom, but because she is the place where Wisdom came to live. The Catechism says that the Church's Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom in relation to Mary, who is acclaimed in the liturgy as the “Seat of Wisdom” (CCC 721).

r.h: The Lord himself will give you a sign
set: The year is about 734 BC. Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel have marched against Jerusalem to force King Ahaz of Judah into their alliance against Assyria (7:1–6; 2 Kings 16:5–9). Their threat is to remove Ahaz and put another man on David's throne. Isaiah has already told the king to stand firm: “If you do not stand firm in faith, you shall not stand at all” (7:9). Ahaz has privately decided to buy help from Assyria instead.
str: vv. 10–11: God offers Ahaz any sign he wants, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven.
v. 12: the king refuses, with pious words.
v. 13: Isaiah's rebuke to “the house of David”.
v. 14: the sign: a woman, a son, a name.
vv. 15–16: before the child can tell good from evil, the two enemy kingdoms will be deserted.
kw: A visible token that God is at work. Ahaz refuses the sign, and God gives it anyway, to the whole house of David.

A young woman of marriageable age. The word does not itself specify virginity. The Greek Old Testament translated it parthenos, “virgin”, and Matthew 1:23 quotes that Greek. The Malayalam POC here has “young woman”.
A name and a promise. God has not abandoned David's house, even when its king will not trust him.
vv: But Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.
It sounds devout (compare Deuteronomy 6:16), but it hides a decision already made. God himself had told him to ask.
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.
Scholars discuss who the woman was in Ahaz's own day; many think of a royal wife, whose son would continue David's line. The prophecy says more than that first horizon could hold.
For before the child knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land before whose two kings you are in dread will be deserted.
The sign has a short-term point: the threat will soon pass. The curds and honey of v. 15 are probably the food of a land laid waste (see 7:21–22).
ch: Matthew reads this verse as fulfilled when Mary conceives by the Holy Spirit and bears Jesus, God with us (Matthew 1:22–23). The Catechism sees here the fulfilment of the divine promise given through Isaiah (CCC 497). The sign refused by a king of David's line is received by a humble woman of David's people. The verse speaks directly of the Son's coming, not of Mary's own beginning, but the feast reads the two together: the mother of Immanuel was prepared by God for this mission (CCC 490).

r.h: He spoke by a Son who became our brother
set: Hebrews is a sermon to tired Christians (“a word of exhortation”, 13:22). Its author is not named. It opens with one long, carefully built Greek sentence (1:1–4), among the most polished in the New Testament. Today's reading joins that opening to the close of chapter 2, so that the Son of glory and the brother who suffers stand side by side.
str: 1:1–2a: two times of speaking: long ago by the prophets, now by a Son.
1:2b–3: who the Son is: heir, agent of creation, reflection of glory; and what he did: purification, and his seat at God's right hand.
2:16–18: why he became one of us: to be a merciful and faithful high priest.
kw: Light shining out from its source. The Son is not a second light apart from the Father. The Council of Nicaea says “Light from Light”.
The mark a seal leaves in wax or a die on a coin. To see the Son is to see what the Father is.

The verb in 2:16 means to take hold of. The NRSV gives “come to help”; the POC gives “took to himself”. St John Chrysostom took it to mean that the Son took on our nature, not that of angels (in substance). Both readings fit what follows.
vv: but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son,
In Greek there is no “the” here: “by a Son”, one who is Son by nature. The prophets spoke God's word; the Son is that Word.
He is the reflection of God’s glory and the exact imprint of God’s very being,
The two images say what the Church would later state at Nicaea: the Son is one in being with the Father.
Therefore he had to become like his brothers and sisters in every respect,
The Son of glory wants a human body, a human family and a human mother. This is why Mary matters: the flesh of the eternal Son was taken from her.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses to teach that in his Son, God has said everything (CCC 65). It uses Hebrews 1:3 for the Son's oneness with the Father (CCC 241). The Council of Chalcedon teaches that he is like us in all things except sin. The feast adds a further thought: the one who would be like us without sin received his flesh from a mother whom God had kept from sin by his grace (CCC 490–492).

set: Mary has travelled to Elizabeth's house and has been called blessed. Luke gives her answer as a song, which the Latin tradition calls the Magnificat, from its first word. It is close to the song of Hannah, who also received a child from God (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and it is woven from the Psalms and the Prophets. Pope Benedict XVI wrote that the Magnificat is entirely woven from threads of Holy Scripture (Deus Caritas Est 41).
str: vv. 46–49: what God has done for Mary.
v. 50: his mercy for all who fear him, in every generation.
vv. 51–53: what God does in the world: he overturns the proud and lifts up the lowly.
vv. 54–55: his promise to Israel, from Abraham onward.
kw: To declare great. Mary does not add to God's greatness; she makes it known. The song begins with God and stays with him.
The key word for today. Mary calls God her own Savior. The Immaculate Conception does not take her out of the circle of the redeemed. She is its first and most complete fruit.
Low condition, not the virtue of humility as such. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Hannah's affliction (1 Samuel 1:11). God looks on Mary's littleness.
vv: and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
The Church does not say that Mary had no need of a Saviour. She needed him as all do, and she was saved by being kept from sin, not by being cleansed after it (CCC 491–492).
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant.
This is the whole theology of the feast in one line: the initiative is God's. Mary's greatness starts in the way God looked at her.
for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
“The Mighty One” echoes Old Testament language for the God who saves (compare Zephaniah 3:17). The “great things” are not Mary's achievements. They are God's work in her.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619). Pope Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854): by a singular grace, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ the Saviour, Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception (CCC 491). St Ambrose, preaching on this passage, wishes that the soul of Mary might be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance). The grace given to her at the start is the grace promised to all of us at the end.

qa: Is the Immaculate Conception the same as the virgin birth?

No. They are often confused. The Immaculate Conception concerns Mary's own beginning in her mother's womb: she came into being through her parents in the natural way, and from that first moment she was kept from original sin. The virginal conception concerns Jesus, conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35; CCC 496–497).
If Mary was without sin, did she need Jesus as Saviour?

Yes, and she says so herself (Luke 1:47). St Thomas Aquinas hesitated over the doctrine for this very reason, wanting to guard Christ as the Saviour of all. Blessed John Duns Scotus helped the Church see the answer: to be preserved from a fall is a more perfect rescue than to be lifted up after it. So the Catechism says she was “redeemed in a more exalted fashion” in view of her Son's merits (CCC 492; Lumen Gentium 53).
Where is this doctrine in the Bible?

No verse states it in so many words. The Church reads it in the enmity between the woman and the serpent (Genesis 3:15), in the angel's greeting “favored one” (Luke 1:28), and in the role of the mother of the Holy One. The Fathers praised Mary's holiness, especially in the East (CCC 493). The Church's understanding grew over the centuries, and the doctrine was solemnly defined in 1854.
rite: The Syriac tradition has sung Mary's purity since its earliest poets. St Ephrem the Syrian (4th century) says to the Lord that he and his Mother alone are entirely beautiful, for there is no blemish in him and no stain in his Mother (in substance, Nisibene Hymns 27). He did not use later Western terms, but the love and the wonder are the same. Among St Thomas Christians the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, the congregation of St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, carry this title in their very name. In the season of Annunciation, we keep this feast while waiting for the birth of her Son. At the Holy Qurbana we too receive him, and ask to be made a fitting dwelling.
study: Wisdom looks for a resting place and God prepares one. How can my family and my home be made ready for Christ this Christmas?
Ahaz refused God's sign because he had already chosen his own plan. Where do I use pious words to avoid trusting God?
Mary calls God “my Savior”. What does it change in me to see her as the first of the redeemed, not as someone far from us?
Why is it good news for sinners that God did something so complete in one of us?
